By Lieutenant Horace S. Mazet, U. S. Marine Corps Reserve

Flying burst upon a startled and incredulous world in 1903, with the Wright Brothers the _dei ex machina_. Yet, by 1906, there were still only two men who could fly.

Almost at once thereafter, however, owing to many contributing causes, not the least of which was an expansion program conducted by the co-inventors of man-flight, a pronounced aviation urge swept over the country which had given it birth. By January 1, 1911, there were at least 1,000 daring men who could fly heavier-than-air machines. Western Europe led all the rest of the world in the promotion and acceptance of this new mode of travel and entertainment.

In America much of what progress there was in the air was traceable to the efforts of an optimistic group who called themselves the Aeronautical Society of America. It is to this body of enthusiasts that the honor goes of being the first actual purchaser of a flying machine. Yet, strangely enough, their program which was admittedly vague and their zealous espousal of a cause yet to be proved, as against years of successful lighter-than-air experiments, evoked general scorn, ridicule, and actual opposition from newspapers and pseudo-altruistic aeronautical groups. Bad luck, also, lost no time in visiting the organization as well as the individual plane builders thereof, while a sneering lack of faith on the part of the public persisted.

But the Aeronautical Society was founded on stern stuff, and saw visions with a practical eye. In all, fifty men in various professions, mechanics, scientists, business men, and wealthy men, answered the call to boom the new society; they believed in aviation and moved with the determination of faith to partake of the achievement spirit abroad in the land.

That American aviation was to benefit from this as yet blind belief in the efficacy of heavier-than-air craft was the fond hope of the organizers. That it did in reality is a distinct tribute to the persistence, unanimity, devotion, and earnest effort which characterized the young society from the start, particularly in the face of denunciatory criticism. The charter declared the intention of the new body to be the fostering and aiding in the development and encouragement of the new art of flying by all means within its power. It was not limited to advice and monetary subsidy alone; members of the unit were fully determined to plunge into the game themselves and emerge either with broken bones and hopes or with airplanes that would actually fly. In particular, members who had recently been affiliated with the Aero Club and its reactionary beliefs in the supremacy of ballooning, were out to show that it was eminently practical to lift one’s self by one’s bootstraps even if, to date, birdmen were themselves a little uncertain about flying machines and their idiosyncracies.

A committee was appointed to secure grounds and sheds for active experimentation. Then a greater step was proposed and carried: to advance aviation in the country, the society invited the famed French airman, Delagrange, to visit America for a flying exhibition that would stimulate the entire nation with the possibilities of flight.

Flying was news; they meant to capitalize on it willy-nilly. If they could not immediately fly, they would get someone who could. And since Delagrange had just made a world’s record duration flight of fifteen minutes, he was sure to “make” every front page in the country.

No sooner was the news out than the opposition countered with an urgent invitation to another famous flier, Henri Farman, whose importation from France was relied upon to produce much revenue and profit for the syndicate of St. Louis schemers and the antagonistic Aero Club. Exhibition fliers at that time were paid no mere pittance, $10,000 for one flight was not unheard of, and as a rule individual airmen would clean up during a year of successful flights, although none of them might have been for more than ten-minutes duration or of greater height than a dozen feet or so.

The society conferred. Feeling that open warfare would benefit American aviation little, the directors moved to withdraw their plan for Delagrange in favor of Farman and his coterie of St. Louis backers with their rosy-tinted publicity. No resentful body was this! When Farman arrived, he was greeted by representatives of the Aeronautical Society which had indeed taken him to their collective heart. Farman was feted at dinners and receptions, while his machine was made ready at a race track at Brighton Beach, Long Island.

Shortly, however, trouble loomed on the horizon. The exhibitions were not paying in cash. People found that the touted flight was more likely a hop—and it might just as well be witnessed from a near-by promontory without payment. Moreover, weather, or rather playful breezes, proved extremely formidable. A slight wind was enough to warrant cancellation of any projected trip aloft. And so Farman, before long, was found in the predicament of having to pay numerous bills which according to agreement, were to have been defrayed by his backers. Time passed and brought no settlement. Farman was threatened with arrest. The remainder of the exhibitions were called off.

But once again the society was ready. On a certain evening, William J. Hammer and Anthony Triaca, fellow-directors of the heavier-than-air exponents, took charge of Farman, packed up his plane and arranged for his safe conduct to a steamer soon sailing for France. Deputy sheriffs with attachments hove in sight, two hours later, but their birdman had flown.

Who could blame Farman for feeling embittered? Yet he later somewhat forgave America, his good nature coming to the rescue, and became an honorary member of the Aeronautical Society.

The first of the week-end gatherings which were to become well known took place at Morris Park in upper Manhattan. A lease had been obtained here until 1911, and it was proposed to use this place for flights and building airplanes. Great as were the soaring hopes on that first Saturday afternoon when members of the pioneering society met to look over the property, none imagined the strides which were to be made within an exceedingly short time. And here again the society contributed to the history of aeronautics, for this occasion marked the first time that any group of citizens had ever leased a bit of land for the purposes of mechanical flight. This was the beginning of the great airports of the world.

There was definite incentive for construction and attempts at flight. A silver cup was offered for the member whose personally built machine was the first in the air. Thus spurred on by the honor of being the first successful builder, the hitherto visionary members were now caught in the throes of a furious spurt of activity. None, dreaming of that gleaming silver cup, imagined the tremendous rise and fall of hopes which were to take place before any member's craft rose in a great struggle from the dark womb of earth and set forth upon wings of its own. On the other hand, none could foresee that within a few months the society was to take the most important step in its career, which would win for America the biggest international trophy in world aviation.

Paying as little attention as possible to caustic criticism from the press and the public generally, the society did not waver. Wilbur R. Kimball, a young genius with leanings toward vertical flight, finally finished the society's first machine. It was an awe-inspiring spectacle. On a frame work of bicycle tubing there was a seat and a small engine. Overhead were twenty-four 2-foot propellers which whirred menacingly on a wide framework. The creation snorted and shook. But this great contribution to the art of flight did not win the silver cup because it could not meet the one condition required: it would not fly.

At the same time almost every other member was hard at work on a machine of his own, or helping another with his idea of what a real sky-traveling vehicle should be. Membership mounted, and soon there was not a vacant hangar to be found. Then, _mirabile dictu_, in 1909 a large number of the members of the distinctly uppish Aero Club of America resigned in high dudgeon at the ruling faction’s anachronistic belief in the divinity of lighter-than-air craft, and joined the Aeronautical Society!

Morris Park, the open-air laboratory, could claim no hill worthy of the name, and some means of imparting initial impetus was sought. The Wright catapult being considered a bit dangerous, a tower was constructed, from the top of which any glider might launch his craft upon the wings of the wind in any direction. As it happened, one enthusiast declined to be disheartened by a lack of breeze. He therefore stayed atop the wooden structure built by Dr. S. B. Battey nearly the whole of one day waiting for favor from the heavens. A building permit for the erection of this tower having been (pardonably) overlooked, the city building department of New York took official cognizance of the lapse, decided that the length of occupancy had converted the structure into a dwelling, and so, as it had neither plumbing nor fire escape, condemned it as unfit for residential purposes and solemnly ordered its removal. It was demolished, and thereafter gliders were towed into the wind by a weight-catapult device as originated by the Wright Brothers.

Increasing interest in aviation, toward which the newspapers were being won over, influenced the society to hold a series of exhibitions of models and plans. Results exceeded the most sanguine expectations.

When cold weather set in, winter quarters for the 200-odd members were opened by invitation in the Automobile Club of America. On February 9, 1909, the first full-dress aeronautical evening took place with enthusiasm running high. Upon this gala occasion Hudson Maxim, later president of the society, gave an address on his views of the future of flying machines in war. Col. Butler Ames, M.C., lectured, and Mr. M. O. Anthony demonstrated his experimental wireless control of airships. Such talks, interesting in themselves, and significant of the diversified tastes of the group’s interests, initiated the lecture series which was to run during the greater part of the society’s history and contributed in no small way to aeronautical progress in America.

With the year 1909, the members felt that it should do something definite to encourage the art on a much wider scale. They turned to a young and promising builder who was making actual flights in planes of his own construction, and doing it very well indeed. Glenn Curtiss was chosen as a fit subject to receive the collective encouragement of the group, and a contract was drawn up, but kept secret between them until Curtiss should officially sever his connection with Dr. Alexander Graham Bell’s Aerial Experiment Association, an organization delving into the physical laws of flight and making abortive efforts to get off the earth.

For the sum of $5,000, Curtiss agreed to build an airplane for the society. The contract thus drawn marked the first purchase of an airplane anywhere, and was the beginning of commercial aviation in the world. The First Aero Syndicate, which purchased this machine, was composed of the following members of the society: Lee S. Burridge, William J. Hammer, Orrel Parker, Louis R. Adams, C. W. Howell, Julian P. Thomas, Herbert C. Smythe, Frank C. Burridge, E. T. Tandy, R. E. Sabin, C. W. Howell, Jr., Frank G. Smith, Jr., E. W. Cameron, C. F. Block- more, Jas. M. Fisher, Carlos de Zafra, Jas. P. Hill, E. T. Birdsall, F. A. Scheffler, O. A. Danielson, J. P. Stalz, Ernest L. Jones, Michael A. Whalen, George Bold, Albert Huth, Wm. A. Kelley, and Dr. S. B. Battey.

Written into the contract was a clause providing for the instruction of two society members by Mr. Curtiss personally in the art of flying. In July, 1909, Charles Wilard, taking his indoctrination on the front porch of the flimsy crates of that bygone day, made his first flight of 500 feet touched the ground, bounced for another 200 feet, and landed safely. Curtiss congratulated him, saying it was a better flight than his own first attempt. An early bird had been born.

The second member to try his luck was Alex Williams, and in his eagerness, he ascended too rapidly, gained 50 feet, and crashed to the ground, fracturing the machine and his arm and thumb, but the damage was repaired without complications and others were soon clamoring for a flight. The society machine in the air was a tremendous impetus to the member builders who still had their eye on that silver cup.

Increased activity was in evidence at the various sheds and hangars of the Morris Park field. A huge triplane was completed by Morris Bokor, and it under went many changes in design before it finally seemed to suit the aberrant aero dynamical convictions of its builder, but it eventually won a prize of $500 for excellence in design and construction at a competition in Arlington, N. J., thus evidently vindicating his judgment. Strange as it may seem, however, the machine never got over its obstinate refusal to leave Mother Earth.

But now the time was coming when the eyes of the flying world would be centered on the International Gordon Bennett race at Rheims, France. The title of world champion automatically festooned the wind-lashed brow of the first across the finish line in this contest, and renowned aviators of all countries planned to flock to the meet on the appointed day. America wanted representation, but the Wright Brothers, premier native birdmen, had disposed of their spectacular airplane to the War Department the fall previous and were occupied with construction work. Mr. Curtiss then approached the society.

Would the society be willing to let him copy their machine for an entry in the international meet? They would. Consequently work started on a replica of the Curtiss-made contraption, while the original was transported to Hempstead Plains, Long Island, where Curtiss practiced flying for the coming contest. Aeronautical and patriotic feeling ran high. Work was pushed on the racing plane, but it did not attain completion in time for it to be flight tested. Nevertheless, go it must, and it as boxed up and sent abroad without having been in the air. Mr. Curtiss followed with the heartfelt enthusiasm of the society and all air-minded America.

Curtiss won! The society's collective hat went sailing into the air also, and now for the first time it felt that unqualified approval was forthcoming from the press and the public at large. It had indeed placed America upon the aeronautical map with a vengeance, and Glenn Curtiss' name became a by-word among news-reading peoples.

Then, in September, the silver cup was finally won. It went to the builders of the Raiche-Crout biplane. Other members' flying machines which actually flew (some of them well) were rapidly completed. Among these were ships built by Pincus Brauner and A. J. Smith, Dr. William Green, whose 2-passenger pusher was the first to employ an ordinary stock model automobile engine in flight, Riggs and Rice (a dirigible), and Frank van Anden. Dr. Henry Walden the flying dentist of Brooklyn, built not one machine but thirteen, the last eleven of which flew. His successful craft were all monoplanes, the first in America. Dozens of other members were fiddling with propellers, engines, gliders, balloons, and parachutes with interesting if not always practical results. There were even wind machines propelled by man power, and glider contests staged at various flying fields in which the society had an interest.

With the advent of the Hudson-Fulton celebration, the society reached a new high in providing amazing spectacles. It was generally agreed that the new art of flying should be brought to the attention of the public, so the society, through its energetic and ubiquitous member William J. Hammer, made all the necessary arrangements and got Wilbur Wright to make a reluctant flight around the Statue of Liberty. This served to focus the attention of the nation on flying, but when, a day or so later, he completed his epoch-making excursion of twenty-one miles, up the Hudson to Grant’s Tomb and around the international war fleet anchored in the river and back to Governors Island, landing within a few feet of his starting point, he stirred the world and thrilled the watchers as nothing else could have done.

A most signal achievement in the society’s history was the banquet at the Hotel Astor on April 27, 1911, at which the President of the United States was the honored guest. Approximately 900 other guests were present, besides the Honorable William Howard Taft. On the speaker’s table was placed a collection of scale model airplanes, and when the time came to clear away after the festivities, Hammer, in charge as usual, could not find his models. The society threatened to turn the hotel upside down unless they were produced, and finally a search discovered them hidden in the tiny room of a German waiter. That is, all except the model of the original Wright plane, which had been made by the Wrights themselves. It had been placed directly in front of Admiral Peary, but everyone denied having seen it after the dinner, and it has never turned up.

Activity afield and in the air was rife thereafter, for aviation had infected many people with its strange virus. Now that America was addicted to watching flying exhibitions, which rapidly became more prevalent, there was a new and more somber note apparent in aviation. It was one of morbidity. Crowds flocked to meets and competitive flights to be sure not to miss a good smash-up. The more spectacular fliers earned for themselves the nickname of dare-devils, and not without reason; they earned for themselves also tremendous salaries when not under contract to exhibition companies. And they sooner or later dove their planes once too often, or tried flying under bridges that were too low.

In fact, by 1912, the situation in the flying world was peculiar. Practically all of the earlier fliers with the exception of a notable few were killed off in the exercise of their profession. As a consequence the public held the general impression that the airplane was hardly better than a device for the perpetration of hair-raising stunts.

It was up to clear-thinking agencies to combat this detrimental impression. Such stigma was exactly what the Aeronautical Society at this time actively had to combat if its years of effort and contribution were to be of lasting value. In this pursuit it therefore engaged as doggedly as it had, four years before, in espousing the cause of aviation itself; papers, lectures, and appearances before other engineering societies geared to the sane promotion of the art were the means. And flying exhibitions, so dear to the heart of every member, were discontinued largely because the society felt that the time was ripe for solid engineering advance rather than for spectacular performances for the public.

Gradually—owing as much to the cessation of flights by members as any one factor—the society began to shift from an experimental and flying body to an engineering, discoursive, consultation organization of practical men. Its mental horizon extended far beyond the flying field, which was comparatively deserted, and the interests of individual members, to encompass the country as a whole and its aeronautical and aerodynamic problems. The society machine had long since been sold.

Members were no longer anxious to spend their money on new airplanes which might not fly well. The consensus of the society’s personnel at the crossroads was, generally speaking, logically in favor of the shift, led as it was by such leaders as Hudson Maxim, illustrious brother of the machine-gun inventor, R. R. Grant, chief production engineer later at McCook Field, Elmer A. Sperry of gyroscopic fame, William g, J. Hammer later of the General Staff, U.S.A., and Gutzon Borglum, and it lent its attention to more basic aviation problems of the nation.

On March 5, 1914, the society in a letter to the Commissioner of Navigation, Department of Commerce, urged the governmental licensing of aircraft operators and the registration of aircraft. Fourteen years later, the government complied.

The entry of the United States into the war threw the organization of the Aeronautical Society into a frenzy of service. Mathew Sellers, Hudson Maxim, and Howard E. Coffin were elected by invitation of Secretary of the Navy Daniels to the Naval Consulting Board in 1917. Because of this the nose of the Aero Club, which had not been invited to participate was considerably out of joint. But its previous constructive history was such that by comparison the Aeronautical Society far outshone its waning rival, and the remonstrance was the last gasp of the Aero Club, essentially a sporting and balloon club.

William J. Hammer was chosen unanimously to go to Washington and become the first outside member of the Naval Consulting Board in 1917, but he withdrew in favor of Maxim and Sellers, with had many friends and were quite familiar with technical details, both being students of aerodynamics. Later, Hammer was pleased that he took this step, for he was called to Washington, and, despite lack of any military experience, was made a member of the General Staff of the U. S. Army with rank of Major, being put in charge of the inventions and patents section of the War Plans Division (I think I am correct), and made frequent flights over Washington with military pilots to test the efficiency of various devices offered to the government. He served with distinction throughout the war. Hammer has also been awarded the cross of the Legion of Honor from France for work he did there with the original French Edison Company in the eighties as head of the European Edison organization.

Other members of the society were Lieutenant Frederick W. Humphreys, U. S. Army (one of first Wright fliers); Captain W. I. Chambers, U. S. Navy; Ralph H. Upson, famous balloonist in international competitions; Lee De Forest, later a famous radio engineer and inventor; Grover C. Loening, builder of the Navy Loening amphibians. Octave Chanute, noted glider, and Wm. Randolph Hearst were honorary members, as were E. I. du Pont, Isaac Guggenheim, F. A. Sieberling, and Inglis M. Uppercu.

Real work for the society—despite immediate and hearty co-operation with Howard E. Coffin under the auspices of the Naval Consulting Board in investigating manufacturing facilities of the United States in preparation for over-seas aerial combat—did not start, however, until General Tasker Bliss asked that a committee of the society come to Washington to confer on designing an airplane with folding wings that could run on the highways like an automobile, then spread out its wings and fly. An abortive creation was constructed, contrary to the counsel of the society, but there the matter has lain to this day. The craft never flew.

The problem of the Aeronautical Society to encourage every form of inventive aeronautics and yet to co-operate with the government was considerably complicated in September, 1917, when aircraft manufacturers pooled all patents. The society vigorously protested against this arrangement as being apt to delay the development of aircraft and stifle invention in the field. Yet in the exigency of war time there were none to heed the cries of those whose toes were trampled, and the society had to swallow its pride along with the opinion of the attorney general on this matter, asked for by Secretary of War Newton D. Baker as a result of the protest.

Activities of the society reached a peak about the beginning of 1918. The aeronautical program, for the execution of which Congress had appropriated $640,000,000, by this time had practically collapsed. Liberty engines were not forthcoming; casualties in training camps were excessive; factories produced few training planes. Still, optimistic reports were constantly issuing from the publicity, departments of the government.

The society met, and urged that something be done. It was decided at that unlucky meeting to co-operate with Mr. Gutzon Borglum, society member, famous sculptor, and friend of President Wilson.

Borglum wrote to Wilson, telling him of the society’s grave doubts as to whether all that could be done was in fact being done in aircraft production.

The President replied in a short letter, instructing Borglum to investigate the situation. The sculptor, no coward, took him at his word, used the letter freely as an “open sesame,” and began his campaign. Being an artist and not a politician he gave out the results of his investigation in the form of an interview with the press.

The papers published the interview in anything but temperate language, and it produced an impression similar to that of an aerial bomb dropped on a gasoline dump. The main facts—or at least some of them—in the Borglum indictment were unquestionably correct. Others, however, were merely garbled or gossip. Thus the danger was that disproval of parts of the criticism might lead to a general conviction that all was serene in the government aircraft departments.

Under such tense conditions the report of the Aeronautical Society, based upon the Borglum findings, was published in April, 1918. It was introduced to the public in a rather spectacular meeting in New York, where one of the speakers was Representative John Q. Tilson of Connecticut. The entire report was republished as a United States document and it led to the appointment of Mr. Charles Evans Hughes, now Chief Justice, as an investigator of the aircraft situation. But no definite action was taken, other more pressing matters cropping up before long.

The result of the publication of their aircraft report on the fate of the Aeronautical Society was disastrous. Official Washington’s attitude was such that many members connected with the war-time government had to resign. All official courtesies were removed, and the society was no longer invited to participate in the development of engineering problems for the aircraft administration and the fighting branches. The usefulness of the society had indeed passed, and even the meetings were no longer held.

The Aeronautical Society in its heyday performed a very essential service by popularizing the possibilities of heavier-than-air craft and by materially encouraging American inventors in the perfection of their devices. Regardless of war-time disfavor, the society also performed a patriotic service in many administrative branches, not the least of which was that very act of calling to public attention certain defects in the government's program of aircraft construction. For these were ultimately remedied.

And finally, the wind-up, decline, and disintegration of the society after the Armistice was largely natural in view of the general tendency in those days to shun all that reminded the country of war. It was the dawn of the Aviation Age.

_As a new decade approaches, we here at ATM thought it a good time to reflect on the last—asking Smithsonian curators to weigh in on their favorite exhibits and acquisitions since 2000._

Stonehenge, a Monument of Mystery: Unearthing Its Ancient Purpose and Power

On this morning, 106 years ago, powered flight was born. Wilber and Orville Wright made four successful flights above Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, in the flyer they had built in their Dayton, Ohio-bicycle shop. To commemorate the anniversary of these [first flights](http://www.firstflight.org/), there is an annual celebration at the site. Tom Crouch, Senior Curator of Aeronautics at the National Air and Space Museum, has attended all but one since 1978 (he has been with NASM since 1974). He has authored four books on the Wright brothers, including a full-scale biography, and was even born in the inventors' hometown of Dayton. I caught up with Crouch before he headed south for this year's event.

**What were you working on at the turn of the last decade?**

In June 2000, President Clinton appointed me Chair of the First Flight Centennial Federal Advisory Board. The board consisted of 18 members, some appointed by the White House, some by members of the House of Representatives and some by members of the Senate. It was a diverse group that included such leading aerospace personalities as Neil Armstrong and Patty Wagstaff, three-time national aerobatic champion. Our job was to work with the congressionally mandated First Flight Centennial Commission to assist in planning a broad-based national celebration of the 100th anniversary of the first powered flight of the Wright brothers. Our organization helped to plan a variety of commemorative programs, including: scholarly symposia, a pioneering website filled with information on the history of flight (which continues to operate today), a national tour of historic aircraft, major air shows and exhibitions across the country, and a host of local centennial events and projects. The celebration culminated at the Wright Brothers National Memorial in Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, on the anniversary date, December 17, 2003. That event was attended by tens or thousands of people, including President Bush (who had re-appointed me to chair the advisory board). As each and every one of those attendees can attest, it poured down rain for a good part of the day, preventing a flight by a full-scale piloted model of the original airplane long planed as the capstone of the event. Even the weather could not take the edge off that day, however. I will never forget the huge crowd, nor their enthusiastic appreciation for the Wright brothers and what they accomplished. It was certainly a highlight of my career.

**What was your favorite exhibit of the last ten years? Why?**

On December 15, 2003, just three days before the big celebration at Kitty Hawk, we opened the Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center at Dulles International Airport. The staff of the National Air and Space Museum had been working on that project for almost two decades. The new facility, so big that our Museum on the Mall would fit inside it, contained over eighty aircraft that had been in storage at the Paul E. Garber facility in Suitland. Today that number has more than doubled. It is the largest and most diverse collection of civil and military air and space craft on display anywhere in the world. How could that not be my favorite? In terms of more traditional exhibitions, I would have to put several of my colleagues efforts high on the list: Peter Jakab and designer Barbara Brennan broke new ground with “[The Wright Brothers and the Invention of the Aerial Age](http://www.nasm.si.edu/wrightbrothers/),” an exhibition developed while I was serving on the First Flight Centennial Advisory Board. Not only did they put the invention of the airplane in a useful technical, social and cultural context, but they placed the world’s first airplane in the center of the gallery, where visitors can see it as never before. Today, the 1903 Flyer is surrounded by exhibit materials that enable visitors to understand the details of the machine—why it is built as it is. Just brilliant! I can’t close without also noting my colleague Bob Van Der Linden’s new gallery—“[America by Air](http://www.nasm.si.edu/exhibitions/gal102/index.cfm).” Exploring the evolution of modern air transportation, it is a giant leap beyond what came before.

**What was your favorite addition to the collection in the past decade?**

Actually, my favorite acquisition is relatively recent, a large oil painting entitled, “Fledglings.” It is the sort of artistic masterwork that you don’t expect to find in an air and space museum. In early November 1908, young Rudolph Dirks took the subway from his Manhattan walk-up out to Morris Park, in the Bronx, to attend an aeronautical exhibition and meet sponsored by the Aeronautical Society of New York—the first event of its kind in the nation. Born in Germany, Dirks had immigrated to the U.S. with his parents and settled in Chicago. A talent for art took him to New York, where he found work as a newspaper cartoonist—the founder of the comic strip, “The Katzenjammer Kids.” Dirks were a serious artist, as well. He painted with Walt Kuhn, exhibited his work at the famous 1913 Armory Show, and was associated with the artists of the “Ash Can” school. The artist was one of 20,000 New Yorkers who attended the air meet that day. He was so overwhelmed by the spectacle that he raced back to his studio, removed a long linen window shade to use as a canvas and began to paint. The resulting work, measuring some six feet long, is a wonderful depiction of the first outdoor air meet and exhibition in the U.S. It is filled with color, with a long line of gliders stretching out on the ground in front of the grandstand. He filled the painting with scores of wonderful, whimsical New Yorkers getting their first look at the wonders of the age of flight. It is on par with European paintings of early aircraft by artists like Henri Rousseau, the sort of modern masterpiece that I never expected to be able to bring into the NASM art collection. Thanks to the generosity of John Dirks, the artist’s son, we will be able to share it with visitors when it goes on display in the NASM [Early Flight Gallery](http://www.nasm.si.edu/exhibitions/gal107/) early next year.

**What has surprised you the most about how your job has changed in the last 10 years?**

I rotated out of the Aeronautics chairmanship in 1999, ending a fifteen year period during which I served as an administrator/manager in both the NMAH and NASM. In truth, I was never all that happy heading divisions or departments. I am a curator/scholar at heart. What I like best is to research, write, collect and share my own passion for the early history of flight with others through publications, exhibitions, talks and other public programs. I am lucky enough to get paid for doing what I love to do!

**What anniversaries, events or people are you looking forward to commemorating with an exhibit in the coming decade?**

I seem to have spent a significant portion of my career celebrating anniversaries. I suppose I am something of a specialist in that regard. Before coming to the Smithsonian I managed the State of Ohio’s effort to celebrate the bicentennial of the American Revolution. Over the past decades, I have been involved in celebrating the Bicentennial of the balloon, the Bicentennial of the Treaty of Paris, the Bicentennial of the Constitution, The Centennial of Flight and the centennial of a string of Wright brother’s anniversaries, from the first practical airplane (1905) to the first flight of a passenger (1908) and the first sale of an airplane to the U.S. Army (1909). Now I am a member of a committee planning the centennial of the first soaring flight (1911). At NASM, I am working with staff members of the National Museum of the Marine Corps to prepare an art exhibition for 2012 commemorating one hundred years of USMC aviation. We are also opening discussions with colleagues from the NMAH on the possibility of exhibitions on the centennial of World War I. Finally, slowly but surely, I am developing plans for yet another future exhibition: "Faces of Flight: Portraits from the Collection of the National Air and Space Museum.” After decades of research, I am finally beginning to write a biography of the first American to fly, a Boston doctor who fought with the British during the American Revolution and ballooned across the English Channel with Jean Pierre Blanchard in 1785. He was a fascinating guy whom I have chased through archives and libraries on two continents. The tentative title is _The Loyal American: A life of John Jeffries, M.D., 1745-1819._

_Stay tuned for more interviews in the coming weeks._

No fan of aviation, Rudolph Dirks was persuaded by a friend to attend the air meet. The “bizarre carnival atmosphere” delighted the artist, who rushed home to paint “The Fledglings,” considered the first serious artistic attempt to depict aircraft flight. NASM

On November 3, 1908, Rudolph Dirks, a 31-year-old newspaper artist, cartoonist, and aspiring painter, joined 20,000 fellow New Yorkers streaming out of their urban neighborhoods and heading to Morris Park in the Bronx. Notices distributed around the city over the past week had announced that the well-known horse and automobile racetrack was now an “aerodrome,” the site of an exhibition and tournament sponsored by the Aeronautic Society of New York.

The program for the event sounded promising. A five-cent, 40-minute subway ride from Manhattan plus a 50-cent entrance fee would give spectators a look at the wonders of the dawning aerial age. Advertised were “distance races for gliders” and “wind wagon pursuit races,” men shot from catapults, and competitions between balloon and parachute descents.

Not one of the powered machines on display would leave the ground that day, or any other, and the only glider pilot to take to the sky during the meet, 16-year-old Laurence Lesh, ended up with a broken ankle. Still, the crowd was treated to the sight of balloons and kites in the air, and was able to examine the winged craft up close.

Rudy Dirks, more excited by the crowd than by the flying machines, rushed back to his 14th Street studio eager to capture the scene while it was fresh in his mind. With no prepared canvas available, he tore down a large linen window shade, stretched it, and began a large oil painting, which he would title “The Fledglings.” While he had serious aspirations as an artist, he was already famous as the creator of the pioneering comic strip “The Katzenjammer Kids,” and that background shows. The painting he started that day has the feel of a single frame of a comic strip, with the lively crowd surging across the scene, milling around the aircraft, and even climbing into the trees.

More than any photograph of the period, Dirks’ painting captures the energy of a crowd gathered for their first glimpse of winged craft, which were just beginning to carry humans into the air. Across the painting stretches a fantastic assortment of flying machines. Most are the work of dreamers whose imaginations were not yet bound by technological reality. Still, some of the craft were airworthy. The biplane on the right of the canvas is obviously one of the large gliders constructed by the brothers Adolph and Charles Wittemann, who had begun advertising themselves as aeronautical engineers, based on Staten Island, as early as 1906.

The biplane glider with the wingtips drawn together, second from the left, is almost certainly Laurence Lesh’s aircraft. For those in attendance, the red automobile poised to tow the glider aloft would have been one of the big draws. It is the Thomas Flyer, just back from its victory in a New York-to-Paris race in which it had traveled west across North America, Asia, and Europe.

By squinting and using some imagination, we might guess that the high-wing craft, second from the right, with one group of men pulling it and a fellow at the rear pushing, is a glider that Aeronautic Society member Louis Adams purchased from Gustave Albin Whitehead, a controversial figure from Bridgeport, Connecticut, who claimed to have flown a powered aircraft two years before the Wrights. If he had, he must have forgotten the secret of his accomplishment, for there is no indication that Whitehead, who lived to see Lindbergh fly the Atlantic, ever left the ground again.

The strange craft with the drooping biplane wings (far left) may well be a large model produced by Arthur Mitchell. Perhaps Dirks’ memory of the wing configuration was incorrect, or perhaps the craft had suffered a serious accident, as the figure in the tree and the individuals clustered at the rear of the machine suggest.

Over the next few years, Henri Rousseau, Pablo Picasso, Robert Delaunay, and a handful of other European artists would begin to portray the impact winged flight had on society and culture. But Rudy Dirks led the way. “The Fledglings” pre-dates the work of those far better known painters, and stands as the earliest serious artistic reaction to the dawn of the air age. Thanks to the generosity of John Dirks, the painter’s son, “The Fledglings” is now in the collection of the National Air and Space Museum, and will soon be displayed in the Museum’s Early Flight gallery.

# Use Wingman to Stay Safe on the Water This Summer 

It’s a fact of summer that people who wouldn’t dream of getting on a motorcycle or bicycle without a helmet, who wouldn’t dare drive without their seat belts, and who routinely look three times— right, left, right —before crossing any street, approach water safety as just a day at the beach. 

According to statistics from the  Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , 10 people die daily from unintentional drowning. Of these two are under the age of 14. Or put another way: eight out of 10 people who drown each day are 15 or older, and the majority of these drowning victims are males. 

More to the point of the Wingman culture, on the  Air Force Reserve Wingman Toolkit  it states that “mishap prevention also depends on responsible behavior.” Often, that means looking out for the other guy. 

Don’t swim alone…but don’t let ot hers swim alone. What looks like the perfect place to dive into the river and cool 

off, is too shallow, too deep, too rocky, too swift. Who knows? If you have a Wingman and there’s a mishap, you’re less 

likely to sustain a fatal injury. It gives one the edge in mitigating the dangers. 

Boating is another source of summer fun and summer danger. The Coast Guard reports that in nearly 85 percent of drownings that are a direct result of a boating mishap, the victim was not wearing a life vest. Add the fact that alcohol use is the leading contributing factor in fatal boating accidents, and the role of the Wingman comes into sharper focus. 

The deadliest factor in summer drownings is lack of swimming ability. For years, the  American Red Cross  has offered age-appropriate swimming and water safety classes in just about every zip code. While learning to swim plays a major role in staying safe in any body of water, having someone with you who knows what to do in case of emergency yields big benefits. Being prepared for the unexpected and by knowing CPR and basic first aid, fatalities and serious injury can be averted. 

Learning what the warning flags at the beach mean is an easy way to stay safe. A large blue flag being blown by a stiff off-shore wind means…what?..Hurricane? Shark? Riptide? Sometimes the Wingman is the person in the lifeguard chair, 

whether you know his name or not. 

Yet, accidents happen, whether your Wingman is there or not. Anticipating that, and thinking the unthinkable beforehand can go a long way in emergency preparedness. These five safety tips help avert trouble and make sure that summertime memories are happy ones: 

If a child is missing, check the pool, hot tub or shoreline first. Seconds count. 

Know CPR and when to use it. 

Avoid alcohol use. It impairs judgment, balance and coordination. 

Keep a fully charged cell phone handy, and know when to call 911 and when and how to call the Coast Guard for help. Know your location. 

Check the weather before you venture out, and be ready to head indoors if a sudden storm arises.

Loreto Playground
=================

### Loreto Playground

This text is part of Parks’ [Historical Signs Project](https://www.nycgovparks.org/sub_your_park/historical_signs.html) and can be found posted within the park. 

**What was here before?**

This playground stands on the site of the Woodmansten Inn, the former mansion of the Pearsall Family. In the 1920s, the Inn became a roadhouse presenting music by great performers of the era before it burned down in the 1930s. Another section of the park was once the grandstand for the fabled Morris Park Racetrack built in 1888 and owned by businessman and thoroughbred horseracing enthusiast John A. Morris (1836-1895). The complex included a racetrack, stables, and a five-story clubhouse in the style of a Pompeiian villa. Before it closed in 1904, it was the most fashionable attraction in the Bronx at its peak.

The City of New York acquired this site for development in 1907. In July 1908, the Aeronautic Society of New York leased the racetrack from the City and used it to hold the world's first public air meet. The airfield remained in operation through December 1910, after which the land was divided into 3,019 lots and auctioned off.

**How did this site become a playground?**

The City of New York acquired the property for Loreto Playground by condemnation for park purposes in 1949 and it opened in 1951. In 1988, lighting was installed in the playground to allow for evening sports. In 1997, the playground and play equipment were upgraded. For several years, the playground featured a roller hockey rink, which was upgraded in 2000 and 2005, though usage of the rink declined and by 2015 plans were made for its removal. In 2021, it was replaced by a multi-use field for baseball and soccer and a walking track.

**Who is this playground named for?**

This playground honors slain New York City Police Officer Alfred Loreto (1902-1950). On the evening of July 21, 1950, Loreto was off-duty and standing near his home on nearby Hering Avenue when he saw two armed men kidnapping a neighbor. Loreto pursued the two escaping gunmen and rescued the victim but was shot during the pursuit and later succumbed to his injuries. At the community’s urging, the City named the playground for Loreto the next year. At a 1985 ceremony commemorating the 35th anniversary of Loreto's courageous act, a plaque was installed in the playground honoring Loreto and all other New York City police officers who died in the line of duty.
